9. Enzyme bio-polishing

P9 · Pretreatment
high

A cellulase bath at about 55 °C for about 60 minutes hydrolyses protruding cotton fibre ends; the jet's nozzle shear knocks the weakened fuzz off, giving a clean, pill-resistant face. Increasingly combined with the peroxide-kill bath.

wet / dry wetwater 8 L/kglane cottondrain machine drain to equalisation

Machines

  • the same dyeing machine

Chemicals in the bath

  • acid cellulase
  • acetic acid or buffer to pH 4.5-5.5
  • non-ionic wetter

Water figuresShibly: enzyme bath about 4 L/kg plus normal wash about 4.

Why fibres come off hereThis stage exists to remove surface fibre into the water, by enzymatic cutting plus abrasion. No published count found; graded high from what the step is for.

Evidenceunknown; no stage-specific study located

Measured todayweight loss (1-3%), pilling grade, strength loss, pH, temperature

A sensor hereCotton fibre (not plastic), mildly acidic, 55 °C: chemically the gentlest wet drain and probably the fibre-richest per litre on a cotton line. A good calibration point, and the control that shows what a sensor does with non-plastic fibre.

Sources doi.org/10.15406/jteft.2020.06.00232

Dyeing

Colour goes in. Jet or soft-flow machines tumble the fabric in hot liquor for hours, then rinse and soap it; the largest share of wet-process fibre release measured.

10. Exhaust dyeing

P10 · Dyeing
high

Fabric ropes circulate through a nozzle for 1-4 hours while dye and auxiliaries are dosed. Cotton takes reactive dyes at 60 °C with 40-80 g/L salt then soda ash, and classical reactive dyes fix only 60-70%, so 30-40% goes to drain. Polyester takes disperse dyes at 130 °C under pressure, then a reduction clear. Blends run two baths or one bath in two steps. Some cotton knits are pad-batch dyed instead.

wet / dry wetwater 8 L/kglane shareddrain machine drain to equalisation, hot drops sometimes through a heat exchanger

Machines

  • jet / soft-flow / airflow dyeing machine

Chemicals in the bath

  • reactive or disperse dyes
  • NaCl or Na2SO4
  • Na2CO3
  • levelling or dispersing agents
  • acetic acid
  • hydrosulphite

Water figuresBAT: batch dyeing of fabric 10-150 for the whole cycle. Shibly: the dye bath alone is about 4 L/kg per fill at 1:7; the whole scour-to-unload cycle is 60 L/kg for a light shade and 81 for a deep one, most of it rinses (see the next stage).

Why fibres come off hereThe longest mechanical exposure of the whole route: hours of nozzle shear and rope-to-rope rubbing at high temperature, while alkali and heat swell cotton and soften polyester.

EvidenceWang 2023: dyeing is 95% of wet-process release; release falls with white shades, lower temperature and shorter time. Badruddin 2026: dyeing about 800 fibres per gram, the largest stage. Zhou 2020: up to 54,100 fibres/L in printing-and-dyeing wastewater. Zhu 2025: three printing-and-dyeing lines were the plant's source.

Measured todayshade (spectrophotometer, delta E), pH, conductivity or salt, temperature profile, bath exhaustion; nothing fibre-related

A sensor hereFibre-rich but dye-coloured, 60-130 °C, salt to 80 g/L, foam. The dye-bath drop is the hardest sample of all; the rinse drops that follow are easier and still fibre-rich.

Sources doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.3c06210 · doi.org/10.1093/etojnl/vgag200 · doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140329 · doi.org/10.3390/w17040574 · doi.org/10.15406/jteft.2020.06.00232

11. Post-dye rinsing and soaping

P11 · Dyeing
medium

Five to ten sequential fill-and-drop baths: cold rinse, acid neutralise, 90 °C soaping to strip unfixed dye, hot and cold washes, until the water runs clear (plus a reduction clear for polyester). This is where most of the cycle's water goes.

wet / dry rinse onlywater 50 L/kglane shareddrain machine drain to equalisation; counter-current or last-rinse reuse in better mills

Machines

  • the same dyeing machine

Chemicals in the bath

  • acetic acid
  • soaping agent
  • NaOH and hydrosulphite for polyester
  • residual dye and salt

Water figuresShibly: 5-10 baths at about 4 L/kg each plus overflow rinses at about 19 L/kg each; 6 of 9 baths (light shade) and 8 of 10 (deep) are rinses. 50 is the balance of the 60-81 L/kg cycle after the dye bath.

Why fibres come off hereFibre freed during dyeing keeps washing out; hot soaping adds further shear time.

Evidencenone stage-specific; the Badruddin 2026 wet average applies

Measured todaywash-fastness, pH of the final bath, colour of the drop water by eye

A sensor hereLater rinses are cool, near-neutral, lightly coloured, low foam: the cleanest matrix that still carries the dye-stage fibre, one drain per machine, batch-discharged, so a count per drop maps to a batch and a recipe. Prime candidate.

Sources doi.org/10.15406/jteft.2020.06.00232 · eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022D2508

Finishing

Hand, softness and shape. Padding of softeners and resins, stenter drying, compacting; brushing, sueding and enzyme washes deliberately remove or raise fibre.

12. Dewatering and softener padding

P12 · Finishing
medium

The wet rope is opened, slit (or kept tubular), squeezed to 60-80% pick-up and padded with softener or resin from a trough; alternatively softener is exhausted in the last dye-machine bath. Out comes damp, chemically loaded fabric ready for the dryer.

wet / dry wetwater 1 L/kglane shareddrain squeeze liquor and trough dumps to equalisation

Machines

  • squeezer or balloon padder
  • slitter
  • padding trough

Chemicals in the bath

  • cationic or silicone softeners
  • wetting agent
  • acetic acid
  • resin and catalyst on some

Water figuresunknown; trough make-up only, of the order of 1 L/kg

Why fibres come off hereSqueeze rolls and nip pressure strip loose fibre into the trough and the squeezed-out liquor.

EvidenceAkyildiz 2024: the drain at the exit of a softening machine carried 0.058-0.251 g/L of microfibre (acrylic and cotton), the only machine-exit measurement found.

Measured todaypick-up %, trough pH and concentration, hand-feel

A sensor hereLow volume, high fibre mass per litre, near-neutral, about 40 °C; silicone emulsion may film optics.

Sources doi.org/10.2339/politeknik.1310805

13. Stenter drying and final heat-setting

P13 · Finishing
none

Fabric is pinned or clipped and dried at 120-160 °C (or heat-set at 180-200 °C for polyester); width and GSM are set and the softener cures. Relaxation dryers tumble tubular cotton knits loosely to pre-shrink them.

wet / dry drywater 0 L/kglane shareddrain none (exhaust scrubber if fitted)

Machines

  • stenter
  • relaxation dryer

Chemicals in the bath

  • none new; softener and resin cure
  • exhaust fumes

Why fibres come off hereFly to exhaust filters only.

Evidencenone found

Measured todaywidth, GSM, residual moisture, shrinkage, exhaust temperature

A sensor hereNot a sensor site.

14. Compacting

P14 · Finishing
none

Steamed fabric is over-fed into a felt or shoe compactor that mechanically shrinks it lengthwise to the residual-shrinkage spec (5% or less) and calenders it flat. Out comes finished roll fabric.

wet / dry drywater 0 L/kglane shareddrain condensate

Machines

  • tubular or open-width felt compactor

Chemicals in the bath

  • none

Water figuressteam condensate only

Why fibres come off hereFelt friction creates lint to the machine housing and later to garment wash if any; not to water here.

Evidencenone found

Measured todayresidual shrinkage, GSM, width, skew

A sensor hereNot a sensor site.

15. Raising, brushing and sueding (not all T-shirts)

P15 · Finishing
low

Wire rollers or abrasive sleeves tear fibre ends out of the fabric face to make a nap (fleece, peach-skin); shearing then trims it. Almost all this fibre goes to dust extraction, but the fabric carries a fibril-rich surface into every later wash.

wet / dry drywater 0 L/kglane shareddrain none (dust collectors)

Machines

  • sueding machine
  • raising machine
  • shearing machine

Chemicals in the bath

  • none

Why fibres come off hereDeliberate abrasion. Processed-surface fabrics carry five times the extractable fragments; abrasion multiplies fragments 5-30 times and fibrils (2-5 µm wide, 30-150 µm long) more than 200 times. The dominant creator of fibre released downstream.

EvidenceCai 2020 (J Cleaner Prod) and Cai 2021 (Environ Sci Technol).

Measured todaypile height, hand, weight loss, pilling grade

A sensor hereDry; but if a mill sueds before garment wash, that wash drain is the place to look.

Sources doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2020.121970 · doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c00650

Garment

Cut, sew, print, wash, pack. Mostly dry; printing and garment washing are the wet exceptions.

16. Cutting and sewing

P16 · Garment
low

Fabric is spread in plies and cut by straight-knife, band-knife or automatic cutter; panels are overlocked and cover-stitched into T-shirts; loose threads are trimmed.

wet / dry drywater 0 L/kglane shareddrain none

Machines

  • automatic cutter
  • straight-knife cutter
  • overlock and cover-stitch machines

Chemicals in the bath

  • none; sewing thread lubricant

Why fibres come off hereCut edges and needle penetration. Scissor- or knife-cut edges carry 3-31 times the fragments of laser-cut edges; a cutting floor sheds 2.9 million fibres per m² per day to the air, and one garment can carry a million fibres, about fifty times a laundry cycle.

EvidenceCai 2020; Raja Balasaraswathi and Rathinamoorthy 2025 (Emerging Contaminants).

Measured todaymeasurement to spec, seam strength, defects; nothing fibre-related

A sensor hereDry; the release shows up in garment wash or the consumer's first wash.

Sources doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2020.121970 · doi.org/10.1016/j.emcon.2025.100559

17. Printing

P17 · Garment
medium

Pigment paste is screened onto fabric or garment and cured dry; reactive or disperse prints need steaming and a wash-off line to remove thickener and unfixed dye. Direct-to-garment printers lay pre-treatment and water-based ink on finished T-shirts and cure with heat; screens and squeegees are washed between jobs.

wet / dry wetwater 10 L/kglane shareddrain wash-off range and screen-wash sink to equalisation

Machines

  • rotary or flat screen press
  • carousel garment press
  • DTG printer
  • print wash-off range

Chemicals in the bath

  • pigment binder
  • urea
  • alginate or synthetic thickener
  • reactive or disperse dyes
  • cationic DTG pre-treatment
  • screen-wash solvents

Water figuresunknown for garments; a print wash-off range is comparable to continuous washing (BAT 5-20 L/kg for synthetics); pigment and DTG printing are dry apart from screen washing

Why fibres come off hereWash-off ranges scrub the printed face; screen washing rinses fibre off screens and pallets.

EvidenceThe '1.39 million fibres/L' screen-printing figure could not be sourced and is unverified. Zhou 2020 and Zhu 2025 bundle printing with dyeing lines.

Measured todayprint registration, colour, wash-fastness, cure temperature

A sensor hereScreen-wash sinks are intermittent, low-flow and thickener-laden; a print wash-off range is continuous and cool, so feasible.

Sources doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140329 · doi.org/10.3390/w17040574

18. Garment wash and garment dye (where used)

P18 · Garment
high

Finished T-shirts tumble in a front-loading drum washer with enzyme, silicone softener or dye for 30-60 minutes at 40-60 °C, then are hydro-extracted and tumble-dried. Used for vintage looks, garment-dyed colours and softness.

wet / dry wetlane shareddrain washer drain to equalisation, often a separate small treatment plant in garment factories

Machines

  • industrial drum washer
  • hydro-extractor
  • tumble dryer

Chemicals in the bath

  • cellulase
  • silicone softener
  • reactive or pigment dyes
  • salt
  • soda ash
  • acetic acid

Water figuresunknown from primary sources; garment washers typically run 1:5-1:10 per bath over several baths

Why fibres come off hereDrum tumbling of cut, sewn and possibly sueded garments; every edge and seam abrades. This is functionally the garment's first laundry, at 25-50 times the release of a consumer wash.

EvidenceWang 2023; Raja Balasaraswathi and Rathinamoorthy 2025.

Measured todayshade, hand-feel, shrinkage, pH; lint filters emptied by hand

A sensor hereModerate temperature, coloured only in dye cycles, silicone can film optics; one drain per machine, batch discharge, easy to instrument.

Sources doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.3c06210 · doi.org/10.1016/j.emcon.2025.100559

19. Pressing, inspection and packing

P19 · Garment
none

Garments are steam-pressed, inspected, folded, bagged and cartoned.

wet / dry drywater 0 L/kglane shareddrain none

Machines

  • steam press
  • tunnel finisher

Chemicals in the bath

  • none

Why fibres come off herenone

Evidencen/a

Measured todayAQL inspection

A sensor hereNot a sensor site.

Effluent treatment

Where every wet stage's water ends up before it leaves the site.

20. Effluent: screening, equalisation, coagulation and primary settling

P20 · Effluent treatment
none

All machine drains combine in a bar-screened sump and an equalisation tank with hours of retention that averages temperature, pH and colour; alum, ferric or polymer is dosed and flocs settle or are floated off.

wet / dry wetlane effluentdrain to the biological stage

Machines

  • bar screen
  • equalisation tank
  • dissolved-air flotation
  • lamella clarifier

Chemicals in the bath

  • alum or FeCl3
  • polyelectrolyte
  • lime or acid for pH

Water figureswhole-mill totals: EU BAT indicative sum for a knit dye house about 20-60 L/kg at best practice; Bangladesh metered 60-81 L/kg on the dye machine alone (Shibly); older winch mills 100-450 L/kg

Why fibres come off hereA removal stage: primary settling captures 38.8% of particles (Prantor 2026); coagulation and sedimentation was the single most effective stage for PET (Zhu 2025).

EvidencePrantor 2026; Zhu 2025.

Measured todayflow, pH, temperature, TSS, COD, colour; online pH and flow are common, TSS by grab or online turbidity; TMC/ZDHC found TSS correlates with microfibre concentration

A sensor hereThe equalisation outlet is the most stable matrix in the mill (35-40 °C, pH 7-9, blended colour) and the only point that integrates all stages, but concentrations are diluted 5-50 times against a machine drain (54,100 fibres/L raw vs 334-1,730 at plant inlets). A compliance sensor, not a process sensor.

Sources www.microfibreconsortium.com/manufacturing · doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140329 · doi.org/10.2166/wst.2018.476 · doi.org/10.1016/j.jes.2026.03.002 · doi.org/10.3390/w17040574

21. Effluent: biological treatment and secondary clarifier

P21 · Effluent treatment
none

Bacteria consume dissolved organics and partly decolourise; fibres are enmeshed in biological floc and settle with the sludge.

wet / dry wetlane effluentdrain to tertiary or discharge; sludge to thickening

Machines

  • anaerobic or hydrolysis tank
  • activated-sludge basin or MBBR
  • secondary clarifier

Chemicals in the bath

  • nutrients (urea
  • DAP)
  • antifoam

Why fibres come off hereA removal stage: secondary treatment adds a further 36.8% removal, 71.8% cumulative (Prantor 2026); aerobic tank, sand filter and BAF showed low removal in Zhu 2025.

EvidencePrantor 2026; Zhu 2025.

Measured todayMLSS, dissolved oxygen, SVI, COD and BOD in and out

A sensor hereThe clarifier outlet is clean and stable but fibre counts are already 70-90% down; good for compliance, poor for process feedback.

Sources doi.org/10.1016/j.jes.2026.03.002 · doi.org/10.3390/w17040574

22. Effluent: tertiary polishing, discharge and sludge

P22 · Effluent treatment
none

Filters and membranes polish suspended solids and colour; zero-liquid-discharge mills push RO reject to evaporators. Captured fibres concentrate in dewatered sludge, which goes to landfill, incineration or brick-making.

wet / dry wetlane effluentdrain receiving water or reuse; sludge off-site

Machines

  • sand or disc filter
  • ozone or Fenton for colour
  • UF / RO skid for reuse
  • filter press

Chemicals in the bath

  • ozone
  • H2O2 and iron
  • antiscalant
  • polymer for dewatering

Why fibres come off hereA removal stage: tertiary raises removal to 95.6%, under 28 particles/L (Prantor 2026); 95.1% overall at Xu 2018; over 85% at Zhou 2020 but effluent still 537.5 fibres/L, enriched in small and coloured fibres; 99% by number but only 67.7% by mass at Zhu 2025.

EvidencePrantor 2026; Xu 2018; Zhou 2020; Zhu 2025.

Measured todayTSS, COD, BOD, colour (ADMI or 436/525/620 nm), pH, temperature, flow, plus permit metals and AOX; no fibre parameter anywhere

A sensor hereFinal effluent is the regulatory point and where a TSS-correlated fibre reading would first be demanded; concentrations are lowest here.

Sources doi.org/10.2166/wst.2018.476 · doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140329 · doi.org/10.1016/j.jes.2026.03.002 · eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32022D2508
